Fields and Constraints

The User model: scalar fields, an enum, and the declarative attributes that replace Eloquent's $fillable and validation rules.

Figure 2.5 is the User model's own fields — its relationships to Ticket, Comment, and the rest are trimmed for now and covered over the next couple of slides.

// Figure 2.5: a plain model (prisma/schema.prisma, excerpt)
enum Role {
  customer
  agent
  admin
}

model User {
  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  name      String
  email     String   @unique
  password  String
  role      Role     @default(customer)
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}

Each line is fieldName Type, plus optional attributes (the @-prefixed parts) constraining that field:

  • enum Role — a fixed set of allowed string values, declared once and reused as a field's type. MySQL itself supports this directly (an ENUM column); Prisma just gives it a name you can reuse.
  • @id — the primary key. @default(autoincrement()) — MySQL assigns the next integer automatically, same idea as Eloquent's default auto-incrementing id.
  • @unique — a uniqueness constraint enforced by the database itself (a unique index), not just application code checking before insert.
  • @default(customer) / @default(now()) — a column default, applied by the database if no value is given on insert.

This is more declarative than Eloquent, where a model class mostly describes behaviour (relationships, accessors, scopes) and leaves column-level constraints to the migration file, written separately. Here, the constraint lives right next to the field it constrains, in the one file that's also about to generate both the migration and the client.
